content:
One widely circulated critique holds that Islam began as a money-making scheme, that it failed to win followers in Mecca, and that it succeeded only after Muhammad (peace be upon him) took up the sword in Medina. The earliest sources allow these claims to be tested against the thirteen years he spent preaching in Mecca.

Below are five points from that period: the offers of wealth that were refused, the roles of Khadija and Waraqa, the size of the early community, the persecution and boycott, and the migration to Abyssinia. Each objection is put at its strongest and then answered.

The strongest form of the claim says that prophethood was a route to riches and rank. The sources record a different exchange. Before his call Muhammad was known in Mecca as al-Amin, the trustworthy, and after it he was mocked. The Quran preserves the taunt that a true messenger would have a treasure sent down to him (25:7-8).[1] Its own instruction to him is to say: "I ask you for no wage for this" (6:90).[2]

Ibn Ishaq, the earliest biographer, reports that Meccan leaders sent a spokesman, Utba ibn Rabia, to offer him wealth, leadership and kingship if he would stop. The Prophet answered by reciting the opening verses of Surah 41.[3] Another report says the Quraysh proposed that each side worship the other's god for a year, and the commentators link Surah 109 to it: "To you your religion, and to me mine" (109:6).[4] A critic can fairly note that these accounts come from the biographies and the commentaries and not from the hadith collections that scholars grade most strictly. Even so, every early source agrees on the direction of the story: payment was offered to him, and he refused it.

Ibn Ishaq also records the pressure brought through his uncle. When the leaders of Quraysh told Abu Talib that he must silence his nephew or stand aside, the Prophet answered that if they put the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left on condition that he abandon the matter, he would not abandon it until God made it prevail or he died in the attempt.[5] Whatever weight a reader gives to the exact words, the report shows how the first biographers understood him: as a man who could have had peace and position for silence, and chose otherwise.

His later life tests the claim more directly. In Medina he governed a growing state, and the hadith describe a household in which a month could pass without a fire being lit for cooking, the family living on dates and water.[6] Aisha reported that when he died his armour was pledged to a Jewish man of Medina for a quantity of barley.[7] A man who sought wealth through religion would have shown it once he had power, and these reports, preserved in the strictest collections, describe the opposite.

The claim names Khadija, the Prophet's wife, and her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal as the planners. Both are real figures. Khadija was a wealthy merchant, and Waraqa, a Christian who knew the earlier scriptures, was her cousin.[8] The question is what the sources show them doing.

In the report preserved by al-Bukhari, Muhammad came down from the cave of Hira trembling and asked to be covered. Khadija comforted him and took him to Waraqa, who said that the angel who came to Moses had come to him, and that his people would drive him out. Waraqa died soon afterwards, and revelation paused for a time.[9] A man following a script does not return home afraid for his own mind, and an adviser who dies within days has no chance to run a campaign. The Meccan Muslims also held no army, no territory and no treasury, so a plan aimed at Persian and Roman treasure had nothing to work with. Those campaigns lay years away.

The critic says the Meccan community numbered under fifty after ten years. No source gives a head-count for any year, so the exact figure cannot be checked, and it is fair to concede that the community was small and outnumbered. What the sources do show is steady growth. Ibn Ishaq lists the first converts in sequence: Khadija, Ali, Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Bakr, then through Abu Bakr men such as Uthman, al-Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talha, followed by dozens more by name.[10]

Two conversions in the sixth year changed the community's position. Hamza, the Prophet's uncle and a man feared for his strength, embraced Islam after hearing that Abu Jahl had insulted his nephew, and Umar ibn al-Khattab, until then one of the fiercest opponents, followed soon after.[11] Abd Allah ibn Masʿud said that the Muslims had been strong ever since Umar became Muslim. Neither man was drawn by money, and both were drawn from the heart of the opposition.

The movement also crossed Mecca's borders. In the last years before the Hijra (the migration to Medina), the Prophet sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr to teach the people of Yathrib, and at the second pledge of Aqaba about seventy men and two women from there swore to protect him.[12] No fighting had been permitted at that stage. The Quran told the believers to bear patiently what was said against them (73:10), and the first permission to fight (22:39) came, by the report al-Tabari gives from Ibn Abbas, as the Prophet left Mecca.[13] The wars of the later period are real history, and the piece 5 reasons why Islam is the religion of peace discusses them. They do not explain how a community formed, held together and won an invitation abroad before any of them began.

Persecution is poor evidence of a profitable fraud, and the Meccan record is full of it. The biographers describe Bilal, an enslaved man, pinned on hot ground under a rock until Abu Bakr bought and freed him, and the killing of Sumayya, whom tradition remembers as the first martyr, together with her husband Yasir's death and the torture of their son Ammar.[14] Khabbab ibn al-Aratt came to the Prophet in distress, and the Prophet reminded him that earlier believers had been combed with iron combs.[15]

The pressure reached the Prophet's own clan. The Quraysh agreed a written pact against Banu Hashim and Banu Muttalib, forbidding marriage and trade with them, and the clans were shut into the quarter of Abu Talib for "two or three years", in Ibn Ishaq's words, until some of the Quraysh themselves moved to end the pact.[16] After the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib, who had protected him, he went to Taif looking for support and was driven out and stoned. Aisha asked him whether any day had been harder than Uhud, and he named that one.[17] Recruits who gained nothing and lost standing, safety and sometimes their lives are hard to explain as clients of a business. Their endurance makes better sense as the conduct of people who believed what they had been taught, and who judged it worth what it cost them.

The claim reads the migration to Abyssinia as proof that early Muslims buckled, and counts fifteen believers against thousands of opponents. The sources do not hide the departure. In the fifth year of the call the Prophet advised the believers to leave for the Christian kingdom across the Red Sea, whose king, he said, wronged no one. The first party was small, twelve men and four women in one count, and a larger group followed: Ibn Ishaq gives the total who went as eighty-three men, apart from the children.[18] The Quran addressed them: "My earth is wide, so worship Me alone" (29:56).

The departure was a flight from pressure, and those who left kept the faith in exile for years, some until after the Hijra. When Quraysh envoys asked the king, the Negus, to send the refugees back, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered for them and recited from Surah Maryam, and the king refused the demand.[19] The fifteen to 4,985 comparison also counts the whole of Mecca as one opposing body, when the reports show clans and individuals split in their response. A faith whose members chose exile over abandoning it has shown the opposite of what the claim says.

The list of emigrants shows how deeply the call had divided Meccan families. Among them was Umm Habiba, daughter of Abu Sufyan, the leader of the opposition to the Prophet, who went to Abyssinia with her husband Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh. He became a Christian there; she kept her faith, alone, in a foreign land, and later married the Prophet.[20] Ruqayya, the Prophet's daughter, went with her husband Uthman ibn Affan. The exiles included members of the most powerful clans of Quraysh, people who had much to lose and nothing to gain.

The bottom line

The Meccan record shows a preacher who was offered wealth and refused it, a wife and a cousin who reacted to the first revelation with fear and reassurance rather than design, a small community that grew steadily, and believers who accepted blows, boycott and exile. Critics are right that the numbers were low and that some believers left Mecca. Both facts are recorded by Muslim sources themselves.

The sword has no place in this period, because fighting was not yet permitted. Whatever view one takes of the later wars, the first thirteen years of the faith were built on persuasion and endurance, and a scheme for profit would have been abandoned long before the boycott ended.

Notes

  1. Quran 25:7-8; Ibn Ishaq, Sira (Ibn Hisham recension), on his reputation as al-Amin before the call.
  2. Quran 6:90.
  3. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1955), "What Utba said about the Prophet"; Quran 41:1-5.
  4. Quran 109:1-6; al-Tabari, commentary on Surah 109, with the report through Ibn Abbas that Quraysh proposed he worship al-Lat and al-Uzza for a year.
  5. Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad, trans. A. Guillaume, p. 119.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 6459, Book of Softening of the Heart, report of Aisha, checked on sunnah.com.
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 2916, Book of Jihad, report of Aisha, checked on sunnah.com.
  8. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, on Khadija bint Khuwaylid and Waraqa ibn Nawfal.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Revelation, the hadith of Aisha on the first revelation.
  10. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. Guillaume, "Ali the first male Muslim, then Abu Bakr and his converts", p. 114 ff.
  11. Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad, trans. A. Guillaume, pp. 131–132 (Hamza) and pp. 155–159 (Umar); Sahih al-Bukhari 3684, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, the saying of Ibn Masʿud.
  12. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. Guillaume, on Mus'ab ibn Umayr and the second pledge of Aqaba, with the count of "seventy-three men and two women" from Aws and Khazraj.
  13. Quran 73:10; Quran 22:39; al-Tabari, commentary on 22:39, with the report of Ibn Abbas and Qatada's statement that it was "the first verse revealed about fighting".
  14. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. Guillaume: Bilal under "a great rock put on his chest", and the family of Yasir, whose mother was killed "for she refused to abandon Islam".
  15. Sahih al-Bukhari 3612 (Book of Virtues, chapter on the signs of prophethood in Islam), the hadith of Khabbab. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 619 (Shamela text), for Bukhari 3612.
  16. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. Guillaume, "The document proclaiming a boycott": "They remained thus for two or three years".
  17. Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 (Book of the Beginning of Creation), the hadith of Aisha, where the Prophet names the day Ibn Abd Yalil rejected him. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, pp. 312–313 (Shamela text), for Bukhari 3231.
  18. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. Guillaume, on the emigrants to Abyssinia ("eighty-three men"); on the first party in Rajab of the fifth year, al-Mubarakpuri, al-Rahiq al-Makhtum; Quran 29:56.
  19. Ibn Ishaq, Sira, trans. Guillaume, the report of Umm Salama on the envoys to the Negus, where Jafar "read him a passage from (Sura) KHYS" (Maryam) and the Negus wept; Musnad Ahmad has the same report.
  20. Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad, trans. A. Guillaume, pp. 99, 146 and 527, on Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh, Umm Habiba and Ruqayya.
